families.blurb: Comes from the Greek word anthropos, meaning “human being.” These words are about people: a misanthrope dislikes people, a philanthropist helps them, and anthropology is the study of humankind.
Comes from the Greek word gamos, meaning “marriage.” Monogamy is being married to one person at a time, polygamy is having several spouses, and misogamy is a dislike of marriage.
Comes from the Latin and Greek word pater, meaning “father.” Paternal means fatherly, a patriarch is the male head of a family or group, and a patriot loves their fatherland.
Comes from the Latin word mater, meaning “mother.” Maternal means motherly, a matriarch is the mother who heads a family, and matricide is the killing of one’s mother.
Comes from the Latin word frater, meaning “brother.” Fraternal means brotherly, a fraternity is a brotherhood, and fratricide is the killing of a brother.
Comes from the Latin word senex, meaning “old.” Senile describes a mind weakened by old age, and a senior is someone older or higher in rank.
Comes from the Greek word bios, meaning “life.” Biology is the study of living things, a biography is the story of someone’s life, and an antibiotic works against tiny living germs.
Comes from the Latin vivere, “to live,” and vita, “life.” Vivid means full of life, vital means needed for life, and to survive is to stay alive through something.
Comes from the Latin nasci, meaning “to be born.” Native means belonging to where you were born, innate means present from birth, and prenatal means before birth.
Comes from the Greek genos and Latin genus, meaning “birth,” “origin” or “kind.” A gene carries what you inherit from birth, genesis is a beginning, and a genre is a kind of art or writing.
Comes from the Greek word psyche, meaning “mind” or “soul.” Psychiatric care treats illnesses of the mind, and a psychosomatic illness starts in the mind but shows in the body.
Comes from the Greek word neuron, meaning “nerve.” A neurologist treats the brain and nerves, and neurotic describes a mind troubled by anxiety — once thought to be a disorder of the nerves.
Comes from the Greek word derma, meaning “skin.” A dermatologist is a skin doctor, a hypodermic needle goes under the skin, and a pachyderm is a thick-skinned animal like an elephant.
Comes from the Latin oculus, meaning “eye,” and the Greek optikos, meaning “of sight.” Ocular means to do with the eyes, an optician makes glasses, and a synopsis gives an overview at a glance.
Comes from the Greek pous (podos) and Latin pes (pedis), meaning “foot.” A biped walks on two feet, a pedestrian travels on foot, and a quadruped walks on four feet.
Comes from the Latin word manus, meaning “hand.” Manual work is done by hand, a manuscript was written by hand, and manacles are chains for the hands.
Comes from the Latin word caput, meaning “head.” To decapitate is to cut off the head, capital means chief or at the head, and precipitous means headlong and steep.
Comes from the Latin word corpus, meaning “body.” A corpse is a dead body, corpulent means having a large body, and to incorporate is to bring into one body.
Comes from the Latin somnus and sopor, both meaning “sleep.” Insomnia is being unable to sleep, somnolent means sleepy, and a soporific makes you drowsy.
Comes from the Greek word pathos, meaning “feeling” or “suffering.” Sympathy is feeling with someone, apathy is a lack of feeling, and a pathogen is something that causes disease.
Comes from the Greek word algos, meaning “pain.” An analgesic takes away pain, neuralgia is nerve pain, and nostalgia is the ache of longing for home or the past.
Comes from the Greek word mania, meaning “madness.” Mania is a state of wild excitement, a kleptomaniac has an uncontrollable urge to steal, and egomania is an extreme obsession with yourself.
Comes from the Greek word phobos, meaning “fear.” A phobia is an intense fear: claustrophobia is a fear of closed spaces, acrophobia of heights, and xenophobia of foreigners.
Comes from the Latin dicere, meaning “to say.” A verdict is what a jury says is true, to contradict is to say the opposite, and a dictator is someone whose word is law.
Comes from the Latin loqui, meaning “to speak.” Eloquent means speaking well, loquacious means talking a lot, and a soliloquy is a speech made alone.
Comes from the Latin vox, meaning “voice,” and vocare, “to call.” Vocal means using the voice, to evoke is to call up a feeling, and to revoke is to call something back.
Comes from the Greek graphein, meaning “to write” or “to draw.” A biography is a written life story, calligraphy is beautiful handwriting, and cartography is the drawing of maps.
Comes from the Latin scribere, meaning “to write.” A manuscript is written by hand, to prescribe is to write out an order, and to proscribe is to forbid in writing.
Comes from the Greek word logos, meaning “word” or “reason.” Logic is the art of reasoning, a monologue is one person speaking, and a neologism is a newly made word.
Comes from the Greek word logos, meaning “word” or “reason.” A word ending in -logy names the study of something: biology is the study of life, and an ornithologist studies birds.
Comes from the Greek word onyma, meaning “name.” A synonym has the same meaning as another word, a pseudonym is a false name, and anonymous means without a name.
Comes from the Latin word verbum, meaning “word.” Verbal means in words, verbatim means word for word, and verbose means using too many words.
Comes from the Greek word phone, meaning “sound” or “voice.” Euphony is a pleasing sound, cacophony is a harsh one, and a megaphone makes a voice louder.
Comes from the Latin lingua and Greek glossa, both meaning “tongue” or “language.” Bilingual means speaking two languages, a polyglot speaks many, and a glossary explains difficult words.
Comes from the Latin specere, meaning “to look.” To inspect is to look closely, a spectator is someone who watches, and retrospect is looking back.
Comes from the Latin videre, meaning “to see.” Evident means easy to see, to envision is to picture in your mind, and providence is a careful seeing ahead.
Comes from the Latin scire, meaning “to know.” Conscious means knowing what is happening, omniscient means knowing everything, and prescience is knowing something before it happens.
Comes from the Greek gnosis and Latin cognoscere, meaning “to know.” To diagnose is to find out what is wrong, an agnostic says we can’t know if God exists, and incognito means unknown.
Comes from the Greek word sophos, meaning “wise.” Philosophy is the love of wisdom, sophisticated means worldly-wise, and sophistry is clever-sounding but false reasoning.
Comes from the Latin credere, meaning “to believe.” Credible means believable, credulous means too ready to believe, and incredulous means unable to believe.
Comes from the Latin word fides, meaning “faith” or “trust.” Fidelity is faithfulness, a confidant is someone you trust with secrets, and perfidious means breaking trust.
Comes from the Latin sentire, meaning “to feel.” A sentiment is a feeling, sensitive means quick to feel, and to consent is to feel the same way and agree.
Comes from the Greek philein, meaning “to love.” A bibliophile loves books, philanthropy is love of people shown through giving, and philosophy is the love of wisdom.
Comes from the Greek misein, meaning “to hate.” A misanthrope dislikes people in general, misogyny is hatred of women, and misogamy is a dislike of marriage.
Comes from the Latin animus and anima, meaning “mind,” “spirit” or “life.” Animated means full of life, animosity is a hostile spirit, and unanimous means of one mind.
Comes from the Latin amare, “to love,” and amicus, “friend.” Amiable means friendly, amorous means showing love, and enamored means filled with love.
Comes from the Latin placere, meaning “to please” or “to calm.” To placate is to calm someone down, placid means calm, and implacable means impossible to calm.

Comes from the Latin gratus, meaning “pleasing” or “thankful.” Gratitude is thankfulness, gratis means done as a favour, free of charge, and to ingratiate yourself is to try to please others to win favour.
Comes from the Latin bene, “well,” and bonus, “good.” A benefactor does good for others, benevolent means kind, and a bonus is something good on top.
Comes from the Latin malus, meaning “bad.” Malice is the wish to do harm, a malfunction is a fault in how something works, and malaria was once blamed on “bad air.”
Comes from the Greek eu, meaning “good” or “well.” A euphemism is a gentler word for something unpleasant, euphoria is a feeling of great happiness, and a eulogy speaks well of someone who has died.
Comes from the Greek dys-, “badly,” and kakos, “bad.” Dysfunctional means not working properly, dyslexia is difficulty with reading, and cacophony is a harsh, bad sound.
Comes from the Greek word monos, meaning “one” or “alone.” A monologue is spoken by one person, a monopoly is control by one seller, and monotonous means stuck on one dull note.
Comes from the Latin word unus, meaning “one.” Unanimous means all of one mind, to unify is to make into one, and unilateral means done by one side alone.
Comes from the Latin bi- and Greek di-, meaning “two.” Bilingual means speaking two languages, to bisect is to cut in two, and a dilemma is a choice between two options.
Comes from the Latin and Greek tri-, meaning “three.” A trio is a group of three, a trilogy is a set of three books or films, and a trident has three prongs.
Comes from the Greek word polys, meaning “many.” A polyglot speaks many languages, polytheism is belief in many gods, and a polygon has many sides.
Comes from the Latin word multus, meaning “much” or “many.” Multilingual means speaking many languages, a multitude is a great number, and multifaceted means having many sides.
Comes from the Latin omnis and Greek pan, both meaning “all.” Omnipotent means all-powerful, an omnivore eats all kinds of food, and a panorama is a view of everything around.
Comes from the Latin magnus and Greek megas, both meaning “great.” Magnificent means grand, to magnify is to make bigger, and magnanimous means great-hearted and generous.
Comes from the Latin word aequus, meaning “equal” or “even.” Equity is fairness, equilibrium is a state of balance, and equanimity is an even, calm mind.
Comes from the Greek hyper, “over,” and hypo, “under.” Hyperactive means too active, hypothermia is a body temperature below normal, and a hypodermic needle goes under the skin.
Comes from the Latin super, meaning “above” or “beyond.” Superior means higher, superfluous means more than is needed, and supernatural means beyond nature.
Comes from the Latin sub, meaning “under” or “below.” Subterranean means under the ground, subordinate means lower in rank, and to submerge is to put something under water.
Comes from the Greek word chronos, meaning “time.” Chronic means lasting a long time, chronology is the order of events in time, and an anachronism is something out of its time.
Comes from the Latin word annus, meaning “year.” An anniversary comes round each year, biennial means every two years, and a millennium is a thousand years.
Comes from the Latin word tempus, meaning “time.” Temporary means lasting a short time, contemporary means of the same time, and extempore means spoken in the moment, without preparation.
Comes from the Latin retro, “backward,” and ante, “before.” Retrospect is looking back, retroactive means applying to the past, and antediluvian means from before the Flood — very old-fashioned.
Comes from the Latin post, meaning “after.” Posthumous means after death, a postmortem is an examination after death, and posterity means the generations that come after.
Comes from the Latin circum and Greek peri, both meaning “around.” To circumnavigate is to sail around, circumspect means looking around carefully, and a perimeter is the line around an area.
Comes from the Latin inter, “between,” and intra, “within.” To intervene is to come between, an interlude is a break between parts, and intravenous means within a vein.
Comes from the Greek tele, meaning “far off.” A telescope sees far, and telepathy is sensing thoughts from a distance.
Comes from the Greek ge and Latin terra, both meaning “earth” or “land.” Geography describes the earth, terrain is the lie of the land, and extraterrestrial means from beyond the earth.
Comes from the Greek astron and Latin stella, both meaning “star.” Astronomy is the study of stars and space, an asteroid looks like a small star, and stellar means starry — or excellent.
Comes from the Latin urbs, “city,” and rus, “countryside.” Urban means of the city, urbane means polished in city manners, and rustic means simple and country-like.
Comes from the Latin word via, meaning “road” or “way.” To deviate is to go off the road, a viaduct carries a road over a valley, and to obviate a problem is to clear it out of the way.
Comes from the Latin vertere, meaning “to turn.” To divert is to turn aside, an introvert turns inward, and adversity is life turning against you.
Comes from the Latin facere, meaning “to make” or “to do.” A factory is where things are made, effective means doing what it should, and artificial means made by human skill.
Comes from the Latin ferre, meaning “to carry” or “to bear.” To transfer is to carry across, to defer is to carry something to later, and insufferable means too much to bear.
Comes from the Latin portare, meaning “to carry.” To transport is to carry across, to import is to carry in, and to support is to carry from below.
Comes from the Latin ducere, meaning “to lead.” To induce is to lead someone into doing something, to deduce is to lead your reasoning to a conclusion, and an aqueduct leads water.
Comes from the Latin cedere, meaning “to go” or “to give way.” To precede is to go before, to concede is to give way, and excess is going beyond the limit.
Comes from the Latin cadere, meaning “to fall.” A cascade is falling water, decadence is a fall in standards, and an accident is something that befalls you by chance.
Comes from the Latin caedere, meaning “to cut down” or “to kill.” Homicide is killing a person, a pesticide kills pests, and concise speech is cut down to the essentials.
Comes from the Latin secare and Greek temnein, both meaning “to cut.” To dissect is to cut apart, an intersection is where roads cut across each other, and an atom was once thought impossible to cut.
Comes from the Latin volvere, meaning “to roll” or “to turn.” To evolve is to unroll, or develop over time, a revolution is a complete turn, and convoluted means rolled together and complicated.
Comes from the Latin fluere, meaning “to flow.” Fluent speech flows smoothly, influence was once a power flowing in, and affluent means having money flowing in.
Comes from the Latin ambulare, meaning “to walk.” To perambulate is to walk around, a somnambulist walks in their sleep, and an ambulatory patient can walk.
Comes from the Latin sequi, meaning “to follow.” A sequel follows the original, a consequence follows from an action, and subsequent means coming after.
Comes from the Latin pungere, meaning “to prick.” Pungent smells prick the nose, punctual means on the dot, and compunction is a prick of conscience.
Comes from the Latin tangere, meaning “to touch.” Tangible means able to be touched, contact is a touching together, and tact is a delicate touch in dealing with people.
Comes from the Latin iacere, meaning “to throw.” To reject is to throw back, to inject is to throw in, and a projectile is something thrown forward.
Comes from the Latin mittere, meaning “to send” or “to let go.” To transmit is to send across, to omit is to let go or leave out, and a mission is a task you are sent to do.
Comes from the Latin pellere, meaning “to drive” or “to push.” To propel is to drive forward, to expel is to drive out, and an impulse is a sudden push to act.
Comes from the Latin vorare, meaning “to swallow” or “to devour.” Voracious means very hungry, a carnivore eats meat, and an omnivore eats everything.
Comes from the Greek archein, “to rule,” and kratos, “power.” A monarchy is ruled by one person, anarchy means no ruler at all, and democracy is rule by the people.
Comes from the Greek word demos, meaning “the people.” Democracy is rule by the people, a demagogue stirs up the people, and an epidemic spreads among them.
Comes from the Latin rex, “king,” and regere, “to rule.” Regal means kingly, to reign is to rule as king or queen, and a regime is a system of rule.

Comes from the Latin grex, meaning “flock” or “herd.” Gregarious means liking to be with others, to congregate is to flock together, and egregious means standing out from the herd — for the wrong reasons.
Comes from the Latin word socius, meaning “companion.” Sociable means enjoying company, to associate is to join as companions, and antisocial means against company.
Comes from the Greek word nomos, meaning “law” or “order.” Autonomy is self-rule, astronomy studies the laws of the stars, and economy first meant the rules for running a household.
Comes from the Latin word miles, meaning “soldier.” Military means to do with soldiers, militant means ready to fight for a cause, and a militia is a body of citizen soldiers.
Comes from the Latin potens, meaning “powerful” or “able.” Potent means strong, a potentate is a powerful ruler, and impotent means without power.
Comes from the Greek word autos, meaning “self.” An autobiography is a life story written by yourself, autonomy is self-rule, and an autocrat rules alone.
Comes from the Latin word ego, meaning “I.” Egotism is talking too much about yourself, egocentric means self-centred, and an egomaniac is obsessed with themselves.
Comes from the Greek theos and Latin deus, both meaning “god.” Theology is the study of God, atheism is belief in no god, and to deify is to treat someone as a god.
Comes from the Greek word zoion, meaning “animal.” Zoology is the study of animals, and the zodiac is the circle of star signs, most named after animals.
Latin animal names with the ending -ine, meaning “like” that animal. Feline means cat-like, canine dog-like, leonine lion-like and vulpine fox-like.
Comes from the Latin herba, “plant,” and caro (carnis), “flesh.” Herbivorous animals eat plants, carnivorous animals eat flesh, and carnal means to do with the body, or flesh.
Comes from the Greek pyr and Latin ignis, both meaning “fire.” A pyromaniac is obsessed with fire, to ignite is to set alight, and pyrotechnics are fireworks.
Comes from the Greek word therme, meaning “heat.” A thermometer measures heat, and thermal clothing keeps you warm.
Comes from the Greek hydor and Latin aqua, both meaning “water.” To dehydrate is to lose water, an aqueduct carries water, and hydrophobia is a fear of water.
Comes from the Greek phos and Latin lux and lumen, all meaning “light.” Luminous means giving off light, to elucidate is to shed light on something, and a photon is a tiny unit of light.
Comes from the Greek word morphe, meaning “shape.” To metamorphose is to change shape, amorphous means without a clear shape, and anthropomorphic means given human shape.
Comes from the Latin mors and Greek nekros and thanatos, all to do with “death.” Mortal means bound to die, morbid means drawn to gloomy thoughts of death, and a necropolis is a city of the dead.
Comes from the Latin novus and Greek neos, both meaning “new.” A novice is new to something, to innovate is to bring in something new, and a neologism is a new word.
Comes from the Greek lithos and Latin petra, both meaning “stone.” A monolith is a single great stone, to petrify is to turn to stone — or to scare stiff — and a petroglyph is a carving in rock.
Comes from the Greek word xenos, meaning “stranger” or “foreigner.” Xenophobia is fear or hatred of foreigners, and a xenophile loves foreign people and cultures.

stories.39: The Latin "abdicare" meant to disown or give up publicly, from "ab," away, and "dicare," to declare. When a king abdicates, he formally gives up the throne. You can also abdicate a responsibility by refusing to carry it.
stories.141: Plato taught his students in a grove of trees outside Athens that was named after an old hero, Akademos. His school became known by the grove's name, the Akademeia. Every academy since, from art schools to police training, borrows that name.
stories.151: It comes from the Latin "accedere," to come near or be added. An accessory is something added, like a bag or scarf added to an outfit. In law, an accessory is someone who joins in a crime without being the main criminal.
stories.331: The Latin "monere" meant "to warn," and "admonere" meant to warn or remind someone firmly. That's still what admonishing is: a serious word of warning. The same root gave us "monster," because strange creatures were once seen as warnings from the gods.
stories.392: The Latin "affectare" meant to aim at or strive for. An affectation is trying too hard to show a quality you want to have. A fake accent or a forced manner is an affectation.
stories.680: The Greek "morphe" meant shape, and "a-" means without, so amorphous is "without shape." The same root gave a name to Morpheus, the shaper of dreams, and from him "morphine." Something amorphous has no clear form you can point to.
stories.682: It comes from Old French "amortir," to kill, from the Latin "mors," death. To amortize a debt is to kill it off gradually, through regular payments. It shares its root with "mortgage."
stories.742: It comes from the Latin "animum advertere," to turn your mind toward something. At first it simply meant to notice. Since people often noticed faults, it came to mean to criticise.
stories.774: In Old English "on an" meant "in one," that is, in one moment: at once. But people who promised to come "anon" so often didn't come at once that the word slid to mean "soon" or "later." "Soon" itself went through exactly the same slide.
stories.795: The Greek "anthologia" meant a gathering of flowers. Early collections of short poems were thought of as bouquets of the finest verses. An anthology is still a collection of the best writing, picked like flowers.
stories.895: It comes from the Latin "appendere," to hang onto. An appendix hangs on at the end of a book with extra material. The small organ is named the same way: a little tube hanging off the gut.
stories.1029: The Arabic "dar al-sina'a" meant "house of making," a workshop. In Venice it became the Arsenale, the huge shipyard where the city built its warships. From that famous yard, an arsenal came to mean any store of weapons, and then any stock of useful resources.
stories.1092: Enemies of a secretive group based in the mountain fortress of Alamut, in Persia, called its members "hashishin" in Arabic, often taken to mean "hashish users." The group was feared for killing powerful leaders, and the crusaders carried the name back to Europe. The drug claim was probably just an insult, but the name stuck to anyone who murders a public figure.
stories.1271: In ancient Rome, an "auspex" was a priest who read omens by watching birds, from "avis," bird, and "specere," to look. Big events began only after he had taken the auspices. To be "under the auspices" of someone came to mean under their protection and guidance.
stories.1272: Roman priests decided whether to start a battle or build a temple by watching the flight of birds. If the birds gave a good sign, the moment was auspicious. The birds are gone, but an auspicious start is still a lucky one.
stories.1300: The Greek "autopsia" meant "seeing for yourself," from "autos," self, and "opsis," sight. In an autopsy, a doctor examines a body to see with their own eyes what caused the death. The word is about being an eyewitness, not about eyes in general.
stories.1326: The Latin "avocare" meant to call away. An avocation was first a distraction that called you away from your real work, your vocation or "calling." Now it means a hobby, something you do for pleasure.
stories.1410: In the 1500s balderdash meant a frothy liquid, and then a cheap jumble of drinks mixed together, like beer with wine or milk. From a muddled mixture of drinks it became a muddled mixture of words: nonsense. Where the word itself came from, no one knows.
stories.1420: The Italian "ballotta" meant a little ball. In Venice, citizens voted by dropping small balls into a box, and the custom gave its name to the vote itself. Today's ballots are slips of paper or screens, but the name still remembers the balls.
stories.1451: It comes from the Italian "banca rotta," a broken bench. Early moneylenders did business at benches in the market. A popular story says a failed lender's bench was smashed as a public sign, though that may be a legend; the "broken" may simply mean the business had failed.
stories.1470: The Latin "barba" meant beard, and the backward-pointing spikes on an arrowhead were called barbs, like stiff hairs. A barbed arrow hooks in and is hard to pull out. A barbed remark does the same: it hurts, and it stays with you.
stories.1504: In the old London law schools, the Inns of Court, a bar or rail divided the hall. A student who was "called to the bar" had passed the line and could argue cases. A barrister is someone who has been called to that bar.
stories.1820: In old private clubs, members voted on a newcomer by dropping a white ball for yes or a black ball for no into a box. Often a single black ball was enough to keep someone out. To blackball someone still means to shut them out, even when no balls are involved.
stories.1853: Bleak first meant pale or colourless; it comes from the same old root as "bleach." From pale, it came to mean bare and windswept, like a colourless winter landscape. Today it describes anything cold, empty or hopeless.
stories.1955: The French called Romani travellers "bohemians," wrongly believing they came from Bohemia, now part of the Czech Republic. In the 1840s the writer Henri Murger used the word for poor, carefree artists living in Paris, and the opera La Boheme made it famous. A bohemian now is anyone, often an artist, who lives freely and ignores convention.

stories.2012: In the 1800s, "pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps" was a joke about an impossible feat. Early computers that loaded their own programs, starting from almost nothing, seemed to do exactly that, so they were said to bootstrap; that's where "booting up" comes from. To bootstrap now means to build something by your own effort, with few resources.
stories.2257: Buff was leather made from buffalo or ox hide. In 1800s New York, volunteer firefighters wore buff coats, and the fans who rushed to watch every fire were nicknamed "buffs" too. From fire fans, the word spread to any keen enthusiast: a film buff, a history buff.
stories.2265: In old English, a "bug" was a goblin or bogeyman, and a bugbear was a bear-like monster used to frighten children. As people stopped believing in such monsters, the word shrank to mean something that keeps annoying or worrying you. A bugbear is now a pet hate, not a beast.
stories.2286: In the 1500s a bully was a sweetheart or a fine fellow, probably from a Dutch word for "lover". Over the next century the "fine fellow" became a swaggering one, then a hired tough, and finally someone who picks on the weak. Only the old adjective "bully for you!" keeps the cheerful first meaning.
stories.2305: In 1820 a US congressman, Felix Walker, gave a long, pointless speech and explained that he was speaking "for Buncombe," the county back home whose voters he wanted to impress. "Buncombe," later spelled bunkum, came to mean talk that sounds grand but means nothing. It's also where "bunk," for nonsense, comes from.
stories.2316: A French "bureau" was first a coarse woollen cloth used to cover desks, then the desk itself, then the office where the desk stood. In the 1700s a French writer joked about "bureaucratie," rule by desks: government run by office officials. The word still carries that hint of endless paperwork.
stories.2327: The Italian "burla" meant a joke or mockery. A burlesque first meant a piece of writing or theatre that mocked something serious by copying it in a silly way. In America it later came to mean a variety show with comedy and dancing.
stories.2400: It comes from the Hebrew "qabbalah," a secret body of mystical teaching. From secret teaching it came to mean a secret group of plotters. By coincidence, the five ministers of King Charles II who ran the country in the 1670s had initials spelling CABAL, which made the word famous, though it existed before them.
stories.2402: A cabinet was first a small private room. The king's closest advisers met with him in such a room, so they became "the cabinet council", and later simply the Cabinet. The piece of furniture with doors and shelves is the same word: a little room for your things.
stories.2413: It probably comes from the Latin "cadere," to fall: the body that has fallen. A cadaver is a dead body, especially one used for study. The word's grim formality suits the medical school.
stories.2417: The Italian "cadenza" meant a falling, from the Latin "cadere," to fall. It names the point where music falls toward its close. Just before that ending, a soloist plays a showy passage, which became the cadenza.
stories.2433: In Latin a "calculus" was a small pebble. Romans did their sums by moving pebbles on a counting board, so pebbles gave us "calculate." Doctors still call a kidney stone a calculus, and mathematicians use the word for a powerful method of calculation.
stories.2461: The Latin "campania" meant open country, a field. Armies set out into the field each summer to fight, and these seasons of fighting became campaigns. Now any planned series of actions toward a goal, from elections to advertising, is a campaign.
stories.2503: The Latin "capitulum" meant a little head, and so a heading or chapter. To capitulate first meant to agree terms set out under headings. Since those terms were usually a surrender, the word came to mean giving in.
stories.2507: The Italian "capriccio" first meant a sudden shiver of fear that makes your hair stand on end, like a hedgehog's spines. It later meant a sudden whim. People linked it with "capra," the goat, an animal that leaps about unpredictably, and that picture suits the word: a capricious person changes mood without warning.
stories.2543: It comes from the Latin "caro," flesh. Carnage was once a heap of dead bodies after a battle. Today it means terrible slaughter, or destruction on a huge scale.
stories.2581: The Latin "casus" meant a fall or chance, how things fall out. Something casual first happened by chance, without planning. Casual clothes are the ones you wear when nothing is planned.
stories.2584: Priests once reasoned through difficult "cases of conscience," from the Latin "casus," case. Some became so clever at it that they could excuse almost anything. Casuistry now means clever but dishonest reasoning.
stories.2703: The Latin "campus" meant a field, and a "campio" was a fighter on the field, often someone who fought a duel on another person's behalf. That's why a champion can still mean someone who fights for a cause. The best fighter of all became the champion who beats everyone.
stories.2748: "Cheap" comes from an Old English word for trading, still heard in the London street name Cheapside, an old market. "Skate" was American slang for a mean, worthless fellow. Put together around 1900, a cheapskate is someone who trades as meanly as possible.
stories.2749: In chess, "check" comes from the Persian "shah," king; it means the king is under attack and must stop and deal with it. From stopping the king came the idea of stopping or holding back anything. To check something is to keep it under control.
stories.2876: Clan comes from the Gaelic "clann", meaning children or offspring. The Gaelic word was itself borrowed from Latin "planta", a sprout or young shoot. So a clan is, at heart, the shoots that grew from one family root.
stories.2966: Where "cocktail" comes from is one of the great puzzles of English. Theories include a horse with its tail docked to stand up like a rooster's, a French egg-cup called a "coquetier", and the dregs of a cask. No one knows for sure.
stories.2967: Where "cocktail" comes from is one of the great puzzles of English. Theories include a horse with its tail docked to stand up like a rooster's, a French egg-cup called a "coquetier", and the dregs of a cask. No one knows for sure.
stories.2987: It comes from the Latin "cognatus," born together. Cognates are relatives by birth. Words are cognates too when they share an ancestor, like English "mother" and German "Mutter."

stories.3040: The punctuation mark comes from the Greek "kolon", a limb or a part of a sentence: the colon introduced the next part. The colon in your body is a different Greek word that happens to look the same. Two unrelated words ended up spelt alike in English.
stories.3064: Greek "komma" meant a piece cut off, and grammarians used it for a short phrase chopped out of a longer sentence. The little mark that showed where such a piece ended took the name. Every comma is still a small cut in a sentence.
stories.3087: "Commit" once meant to entrust something to someone. A committee is the group to whom a task has been committed. The "-ee" ending marks the people receiving it, as in "employee."
stories.3123: The Latin "compendium" meant something weighed together and saved. It was a gathering of many things into a single, handy collection. Now it usually means a book that sums up a subject in one place.
stories.3245: The Latin "conficere" meant to put together, to prepare. A confection was a carefully prepared mixture, often medicine mixed with sugar. Now it means a fancy sweet or cake, or anything elaborately made.
stories.3289: The Romans believed each person had a "genius," a guiding spirit born with them. Someone congenial had a spirit like yours, "con-," together. That's why congenial means pleasant and easy to get along with.
stories.3331: It comes from Latin "con," with, and "scire," to know: knowing something together with yourself. Your conscience is the inner knowledge of right and wrong that you carry around, the part of you that knows what you've done.
stories.3337: It comes from the Latin "conscribere," to write together in a list. Soldiers were conscripted by having their names written on the roll. To conscript someone is to force them to join the armed forces.
stories.3396: In ancient Rome two consuls were elected each year to lead the republic together, so neither could rule alone. The word is linked to "consulere", to take counsel. Today's consuls, who look after their citizens in a foreign city, borrowed the grand old title.
stories.3499: The Latin "conversari" meant to keep company, to live with. If you are conversant with something, you know it as if you had lived alongside it. It's related to "conversation."
stories.3551: Coronary comes from Latin "corona", a crown. The arteries feeding the heart wrap around it like a crown or garland. A coronary, a heart attack, is named after those crown-like arteries.
stories.3637: It comes from the Old French "covert," covered, the same as "cover." Despite the look, it isn't related to "vert," turn. A covert operation is a covered one, hidden from view.
stories.3784: A traditional explanation says that in old English courts, the clerk wrote "cul. prit." as shorthand for French words meaning "guilty, and ready to prove it," and the shorthand was later taken as a name for the accused. Scholars aren't sure this is true. Either way, a culprit is now whoever is to blame.
stories.3834: Curtsy is simply a shortened form of "courtesy". A courtesy was any polite act; the small bow with bent knees, made especially by women, took the general word for politeness as its name.
stories.3860: The Greek "kynikos" means "doglike." It was the nickname of Diogenes and his followers, who lived rough, mocked good manners and scorned comfort, rather like stray dogs. What survives is their scorn: a cynic expects the worst of everyone's motives.
stories.3946: The old French "debaucher" meant to lure someone away from their work or duty. Someone lured away from duty was led astray, and the word sank to mean being led into excess and vice. Debauchery is now wild, shameless indulgence.
stories.3956: It's "de-" plus "bunk," which is short for bunkum, empty talk. The word was coined in the 1920s for showing that a claim or a hero's reputation was nonsense. To debunk is to take the bunk out of something and expose the truth.
stories.4003: The Latin "dedicare" meant to declare something holy and give it to a god. A temple was dedicated to its god. Today you can dedicate a book to a friend, or your time to a cause.
stories.4023: The Latin "deficere" meant to fail or desert. A defect is the place where something fails. To defect is to desert your country or side for another.
stories.4024: The Latin "deficere" meant to fail or desert. A defect is the place where something fails. To defect is to desert your country or side for another.
stories.4032: It comes from the Latin "deferre," to carry down or hand over. When you show deference, you hand the decision to someone else out of respect. It is giving way to another person's judgment.
stories.4057: It comes from Latin "de-," down from, and "genus," birth or kind. Something degenerate has fallen from the qualities of its kind, becoming worse than its ancestors. Today it describes anything that has declined, physically or morally.

stories.4059: It comes from Latin "de-," down from, and "genus," birth or kind. Something degenerate has fallen from the qualities of its kind, becoming worse than its ancestors. Today it describes anything that has declined, physically or morally.
stories.4183: It comes from the French "deporter," to carry yourself, from the Latin "portare," to carry. Your deportment is how you carry your body. Old finishing schools taught it by making pupils walk with books on their heads.
stories.4226: Thomas Derrick was a famous hangman at Tyburn in London around 1600, and his name was used for the gallows. Later the name passed to a lifting crane, whose tall frame and hanging rope looked similar. Today oil rigs use derricks with no grim memory attached.
stories.4377: The Latin "digitus" meant finger, and since we count on our fingers, the numbers 0 to 9 are called digits. A digital clock shows time in numbers instead of hands. Computers work by storing everything as numbers, so they are digital too.
stories.4516: "Gruntle" was an old word meaning to grumble or keep grunting, like a pig. Adding "dis-" here made the meaning stronger, not opposite. So a disgruntled person is someone who is grumbling a great deal; "gruntled," meaning pleased, was invented later as a joke.
stories.4534: "Ingenuous" comes from a Latin word for freeborn and came to mean open and honest. "Dis-" reverses it. A disingenuous person only pretends to be frank, while hiding what they really know or want.
stories.4558: The Old French "desparagier" meant to marry someone of lower rank, which brought disgrace on a family. It comes from "par," equal: it was to make someone unequal. Now to disparage is to make someone or something seem less important, by talking it down.
stories.4579: It comes from the Old French "desporter," to carry away from work. To disport yourself is to have fun and play. The short form "sport" first meant fun of any kind.
stories.4583: The Latin "dispositio" meant an arrangement. Astrologers spoke of the disposition of the planets at the moment of your birth, believing that arrangement shaped your nature. The word came to mean the nature itself: your usual mood or temperament.
stories.4842: Dryad comes from the Greek "drys", oak or tree. In Greek myth a dryad was a nymph who lived in a tree, and in some stories died when her tree did.
stories.4847: The ducat was a gold coin first minted in Venice in 1284. Its name probably comes from the Latin "ducatus," duchy, a word stamped on early coins, from "dux," leader. It became one of Europe's best-known coins.
stories.4849: The Latin "ductilis" meant able to be led, from "ducere," to lead. A ductile metal can be drawn out into thin wire. The word can also describe a person easily led.
stories.4866: John Duns Scotus was one of the most brilliant thinkers of the Middle Ages. Two centuries later, Renaissance scholars mocked his followers, the "Dunsmen", as hair-splitting dullards who resisted new learning. The insult stuck, and a great philosopher's name came to mean a slow learner.
stories.4985: The Latin "aedificare" meant to build. Early Christian writers spoke of "building up" a person's faith and understanding. Edification still means improving someone's mind, as if constructing it.
stories.4986: The Latin "aedificium" meant a building, from "aedes," temple or house, and "facere," to make. An edifice is a large, grand building. It can also mean a big system of ideas built up over time.
stories.4993: It comes from the French "effacer," to remove the face. Rubbing out the face of a coin or a carving wipes away what made it recognisable. To efface is to erase, and self-effacing people keep themselves out of sight.
stories.5105: In printing, an em is a space as wide as the letter M in the type being used. The em dash takes its length from that measure, which is why it is the long dash.
stories.5111: In Roman law, a father held his son "in hand," under his power. To emancipate, "e manu capere," was to release him from that hand, giving him independence. The word later meant freeing slaves, and now freeing anyone from control.
stories.5156: The Latin "emeritus" described a Roman soldier who had served his years and earned his discharge, from "merere," to earn. Today it is an honour for a professor or official who has retired after long service but keeps the title.
stories.5191: It comes from the Greek "empyros," in fire. Old astronomers believed the highest heaven, the empyrean, was made of pure fire and light. Empyreal now means heavenly or sublime.
stories.5238: It comes from the Greek "enkyklios paideia," meaning an all-round, complete education. Renaissance scholars joined it into one word for a book that covers every subject. An encyclopedia is still meant to hold the full circle of knowledge.
stories.5271: It comes from French "en gage," in pledge. To engage was to put yourself under a promise. Being engaged to marry is a pledge, and engaging someone's help or attention binds them to a task.
stories.5340: It comes from the French "entourer," to surround. Your entourage is the group of people who surround you wherever you go. It's usually used for the attendants of someone famous or important.
stories.5547: It comes from the Greek "eu," well, and "kalyptos," covered. The tree's flower bud is covered by a tight little cap, which pops off when it blooms. The French botanist who named it in 1788 picked out that detail.
stories.5562: In 1578, John Lyly wrote a story about a young man named Euphues, Greek for "well-shaped." Its style was so ornate and full of balanced phrases that it set a fashion. Euphuism now means any showy, overdone style of writing.
stories.5695: The Latin "exsequi" meant to follow something through to the end. To execute a plan or an order is to carry it all the way out. Executing a criminal began as carrying out the sentence of death, which is why the word now has both meanings.
stories.5769: It comes from the Latin "expedire," to free the feet from a trap. Something expedient frees you to move forward: it's useful and convenient. The word often hints that the convenient choice isn't the right one.
stories.5770: The Latin "expedire" meant to free the feet, to get them out of a snare: "ex," out, and "pes," foot. To expedite something is to free it from whatever slows it down. Today it simply means to speed up.
stories.5771: It comes from the Latin "expedire," to free the feet and set off. An expedition was first a setting out, with speed and readiness. Now it means an organised journey with a purpose, like exploring a mountain.
stories.5821: The Latin "expungere" meant to prick out. Roman clerks marked names to be removed from a list by pricking dots under them. To expunge something is to wipe it out completely.
stories.5920: The Latin "factio" meant a group acting together. In Rome, the word named the rival chariot-racing teams, the Reds, Whites, Greens and Blues, whose fans fought fiercely. A faction is now a small group inside a larger one, often in conflict.
stories.6054: "Feck" was a Scottish shortening of "effect," meaning strength or worth. Someone feckless had no effect: they were weak, useless and lacking in purpose. The Scottish writer Thomas Carlyle helped spread the word, but "feck" itself never caught on.
stories.6073: A "feist" was a small, noisy dog in American dialect. The name came from an old rude word for a dog that breaks wind. A dog that small yaps and snaps far beyond its size, so a feisty person is spirited, lively and ready for a fight.
stories.6349: The mineral fluorspar was used to help metals flow when melted, from the Latin "fluere," to flow. In 1852 the scientist George Stokes noticed it glowed under certain light and named the glow fluorescence after it. Fluorescent lights still glow that way.
stories.6545: It comes from Old French "franc," free, and first meant a freedom or special right. The right to vote was one such freedom, which is why voting rights are still called the franchise. A business franchise is the right to trade under a company's name.
stories.6547: The Franks were the Germanic people who conquered Gaul, which later became France. Since they were the free people in the lands they ruled, "frank" came to mean free. From free in body it came to mean free in speech: honest and open.
stories.6548: It comes from Old French "franc encens," meaning fine or pure incense. "Franc," free, also had the sense of noble or of high quality. So frankincense was simply the best kind of incense.
stories.6751: In the Middle Ages, the music teacher Guido of Arezzo named the lowest note of his scale "gamma ut." The name came to mean the whole scale, from the bottom note to the top. So to "run the gamut" is to go through the whole range of something.
stories.6799: In 1500s Venice, news sheets were sold for a "gazeta," a coin of very little value. The name passed from the coin to the paper you bought with it. A gazette now is a newspaper, especially an official one.
stories.6804: An old word "geck" meant a fool. In American carnivals around 1900, the geek was the lowest act of all: a performer who bit the heads off live chickens. From that grim job the word drifted to anyone odd, and later to the clever enthusiast it usually means today.
stories.6813: The Danish scientist Wilhelm Johannsen coined "gene" in 1909, taking it from the Greek "genos," birth or kind. A gene is the unit of inheritance that is passed on at birth. The same root is in "generation" and "genetic."
stories.6823: In Latin, "generosus" meant "of noble birth," from "genus," family or kind. Nobles were expected to be big-hearted and open-handed, so the word slowly moved from your family to your behaviour. Today anyone can be generous, whoever their family is.
stories.6827: The Latin "genialis" was linked to a person's "genius," their guiding spirit, and to birth, marriage and festivals. It meant festive and cheerful. A genial person is warm, friendly and good-humoured.
stories.6830: To the Romans a genius was a guardian spirit born with each person, shaping their character and luck. A place could have its genius too. Over time the word moved from the spirit that guides you to the rare gift itself, and then to the person who has it.
stories.6835: The Latin "gentilis" meant someone belonging to a clan or nation, a "gens." Early Bible translators used it for "the nations," meaning peoples who were not Jewish. That's still its main sense today.
stories.6840: "Gentry" were the well-born upper classes, from "gentle," meaning of good family. In 1964 the sociologist Ruth Glass coined "gentrification" for wealthier people moving into working-class parts of London. To gentrify is to make a poor area richer, often pushing out the people who lived there.
stories.6893: The first ghetto was in Venice, where in 1516 the city forced Jewish people to live on one walled island. A likely explanation is that the area had held a foundry, a "getto" in Italian, though no one is sure. Ghetto came to mean any part of a city where a group is pushed to live apart.
stories.7115: Northern English dialect had the word "gaum," meaning sense or attention, from Old Norse. To be gaumless, later spelled gormless, was to have none of it. "Gorm" itself has died out and lives on only inside "gormless."
stories.7133: The Greek "kybernan" meant to steer a ship, and the Romans turned it into "gubernare." To govern a country was to steer the ship of state. The same root gives "gubernatorial" and, from the Greek side, "cybernetics."
stories.7174: During the American Civil War, people spoke of news travelling by the "grapevine telegraph": not by real telegraph wires, but passed from person to person like a tangled, twisting vine. "Hearing it through the grapevine" still means hearing a rumour informally.
stories.7196: The Latin "gratuitus" meant freely given, done as a favour, from "gratia," favour. From "given for free" it shifted to "done for no reason." Gratuitous violence in a film is violence with no reason to be there.
stories.7270: In 1740, the British admiral Edward Vernon, nicknamed "Old Grog" for his coat of grogram cloth, ordered his sailors' rum to be watered down. The drink was called grog after him. Too much grog left a sailor groggy, which now means dazed and unsteady from any cause.
stories.7315: It comes from the Latin "gubernator," a steersman of a ship, which also gave us "governor." A governor steers a state the way a helmsman steers a boat. So a gubernatorial election is one to choose the person at the wheel.
stories.7326: In 1789 the French doctor Joseph-Ignace Guillotin proposed that executions be done by a quick machine, as a more humane and equal method. He didn't invent it, and he opposed the death penalty, but his name was attached to the blade anyway. His embarrassed family later changed their name.
