stories.7392: The haiku grew out of the "hokku", the opening verse of a longer linked poem written by several poets. In the 1890s the poet Masaoka Shiki argued that the opening verse should stand on its own and gave it the name haiku. A starting line became a whole art form.
stories.7400: The Greek "halkyon" was the kingfisher. A myth said that when it nested on the sea in midwinter, the gods calmed the winds for about two weeks. Those calm "halcyon days" became a name for any peaceful, happy time, usually one that is now in the past.
stories.7622: A heckle was a steel comb used to tear and straighten flax fibres. To heckle someone came to mean pulling their words apart with sharp questions, as the comb pulled at the flax. A popular story says flax-workers in Scotland were famous for arguing over the news while they worked, but no one knows for sure.
stories.7625: Hector was the noble Trojan hero of Homer's Iliad. In 1600s London, gangs of swaggering young bullies called themselves "Hectors" to sound heroic. Their behaviour won out, and to hector now means to bully someone with loud, threatening talk.
stories.7650: Heist is simply "hoist", said the way it sounded in some American speech. In 1920s criminal slang, to hoist something was to lift it, meaning to steal it. The new spelling followed the pronunciation, and a heist became a robbery, usually a daring one.
stories.7740: "High" here has an old meaning: open, public, belonging to all, as in "highway" or "high street." The high seas are the open ocean far from any coast. No single country owns them; they are shared by everyone.
stories.7806: It is probably a shortening of "hocus-pocus," the fake Latin words of stage conjurers. Some believe "hocus-pocus" itself mocked a line from the Latin church service. From a magician's trick, a hoax came to mean any deliberate deception.
stories.7918: Latin "horrere" meant to bristle or stand on end, like hair. Horror was first the shudder that makes your hair stand up. The feeling gave its name to the things that cause it.
stories.8069: Greek "hyph' hen" meant "under one" or "together". Ancient grammarians used a small curved mark under two letters to show that they belonged to one word. That joining mark, and its name, became our hyphen.
stories.8077: The Greek "hypochondria" was the upper belly, the area "under the cartilage" of the ribs. Ancient doctors thought low spirits began there. Over time the gloom came to mean a constant worry about being ill.
stories.8078: The Greek "hypokrisis" meant acting a part on stage. An actor wore a mask and pretended to be someone else. Hypocrisy is acting out goodness you don't really have.
stories.8079: In ancient Greece, a "hypokrites" was a stage actor, someone who played a part. Early Christian writers used the word for people who played at being good. A hypocrite still says one thing while doing another, like an actor behind a mask.
stories.8087: It comes from the Greek "hypo," under, and "thesis," placing: something placed underneath. A hypothesis is the idea you lay down as a foundation, then test. If it holds, you can build on it.
stories.8124: In 1796 the French thinker Destutt de Tracy coined "ideologie" for a new science of ideas. Napoleon sneered at his group as impractical dreamers, and the word picked up a political edge. An ideology is now a whole system of beliefs about how society should work.
stories.8153: "Ignoramus" is Latin for "we do not know." English juries once wrote it on a charge they rejected for lack of evidence. In 1615 a play mocked a foolish lawyer named Ignoramus, and the word came to mean an ignorant person.
stories.8269: The Latin "impedire" meant to shackle someone's feet: "in," in, and "pes," foot. To impede someone is to slow them down, as if their feet were tied. It's the opposite of "expedite."
stories.8270: It comes from the Latin "impedire," to shackle the feet. An impediment is whatever trips or hinders you. A speech impediment hinders the flow of your words.
stories.8273: It comes from the Latin "pendere," to hang. Something impending is hanging over you, as if it might drop at any moment. That's why the word is usually used for something unwelcome that is about to happen.
stories.8468: Roman priests read omens from birds before any big event. An inauspicious sign meant the gods disapproved, and the event was put off. Today an inauspicious start is simply an unlucky or unpromising one.
stories.8486: It comes from the Italian "incarnatino," flesh-coloured, from "carne," flesh. Shakespeare used it in Macbeth for staining the seas blood-red. Because of that famous line, it now means blood-red or crimson.
stories.8610: An old contract was written twice on one sheet, which was then cut apart along a wavy, toothed line. Each side kept a half, and the two halves fitting together proved they were genuine; the name comes from the Latin "dens," tooth. An indenture became a binding contract, especially one tying a worker to a master.
stories.8616: The Latin "index" meant a pointer, or someone who points something out, which is why the finger you point with is the index finger. An index in a book points you to the page you need. Even a price index points to how costs are changing.
stories.8617: The Latin "index" meant a pointer, or someone who points something out, which is why the finger you point with is the index finger. An index in a book points you to the page you need. Even a price index points to how costs are changing.
stories.8627: It first meant impartial, making no difference between sides, neither good nor bad. A judge was supposed to be indifferent. Over time it came to mean not caring at all.
stories.8799: It is Italian for "influence." People once blamed epidemics on the influence of the stars. After a great outbreak in Italy in 1743, English took the word for the illness itself, and later shortened it to flu.
stories.8826: The Latin "ingenium" meant your inborn nature, especially natural talent. An ingenious person is full of that talent, inventive and clever. The same root gives "engine," a clever device, and "engineer."
stories.8829: The Latin "ingenuus" meant freeborn, not a slave. Free people were thought to be open, honest and noble. Over time it came to mean innocent and trusting, sometimes too much so.
stories.8896: The Latin "inoculare" meant to graft a bud onto a plant, and the bud was called an "oculus," an eye. Doctors in the 1700s "grafted" a tiny bit of a disease into a person to protect them from it. So a gardening word moved into medicine.
stories.9083: It comes from the Old French "s'entreferir," to strike each other. It was first used of horses whose legs knocked together as they walked. To interfere now means to get in the way of others' affairs.
stories.9234: It comes from the Latin "invidia," envy. An invidious choice or comparison is one likely to stir up envy and resentment. That's why it now means unfair and unpleasant.
stories.9405: The Jesuits, a Catholic order founded in the 1500s, were famous for their learning and skill in argument. Their opponents accused them of using clever, twisted reasoning to dodge the truth. So jesuitical came to mean crafty and hair-splitting in argument.
stories.9443: It is a "keep doing it" form of "joust," the sport of knights charging into each other. Adding "-le" means repeated action, as in sparkle or crackle. To jostle is to keep bumping and pushing, as in a crowd.
stories.9454: Astrologers believed the planet Jupiter, also called Jove, gave people cheerful, good-humoured moods. Someone born under Jupiter was said to be jovial. The belief in planets has faded, but the happy mood stayed with the word.
stories.9460: The Latin "jubilare" meant to raise a joyful shout. It is not related to "jubilee," which comes from a Hebrew word for a ram's horn, though the two have long been mixed up. A jubilant person is so happy they want to shout.
stories.9703: The Latin "lacuna" meant a pit or a pool, from "lacus," a lake. Scholars used it for a gap in an old manuscript, a hole where words were missing. Now a lacuna is any gap in something that should be complete.
stories.9706: In Old English, "hlaefdige" meant "loaf-kneader," the woman of the house who made the bread. A "lord" was the "hlafweard," the loaf-guardian. The loaf has long since disappeared from both words, which now speak of rank and good manners.
stories.9712: It comes from the Italian "laguna," from the Latin "lacuna," a pit or pool. The most famous one is the lagoon of Venice, the shallow water the city stands in. A lagoon is a stretch of shallow water cut off from the sea.
stories.10209: The word joins Greek "lykos", wolf, and "anthropos", human. In Greek myth King Lycaon served human flesh to Zeus at a feast, and Zeus punished him by turning him into a wolf. His name and the werewolf idea have run together ever since.
stories.10240: Greek "magma" meant a thick paste or kneaded mass, from a verb meaning to knead, like dough. Chemists used it for any soft, doughy mixture. Geologists later borrowed it for the molten rock that churns beneath the Earth's crust.
stories.10320: It comes from the Latin "mandare," to put into someone's hand, from "manus," hand. A mandate is a task or command entrusted to someone. When voters give a government a mandate, they put that power into its hands.
stories.10321: It comes from the Latin "mandare," to put into someone's hand, from "manus," hand. A mandate is a task or command entrusted to someone. When voters give a government a mandate, they put that power into its hands.
stories.10328: The Old French "manuevre" meant work done by hand, from the Latin "manus," hand, and "operari," to work. It became a term for the careful movement of troops or ships. Now a maneuver is any skilful move, often a sly one.
stories.10329: The Old French "manuevre" meant work done by hand, from the Latin "manus," hand, and "operari," to work. It became a term for the careful movement of troops or ships. Now a maneuver is any skilful move, often a sly one.
stories.10361: It comes from the Latin "manu mittere," to send from the hand. A Roman master freed a slave in a ceremony that released them from his control. To manumit still means to set a slave free.
stories.10404: In 1886 the doctor Richard von Krafft-Ebing named this condition after the Austrian novelist Leopold von Sacher-Masoch, whose stories featured characters who wanted to suffer. Sacher-Masoch was still alive, and he was not pleased. Today the word also means enjoying hardship in general.
stories.10430: The Latin "matricula" was a public list or register. To matriculate was to have your name entered on the list. Universities kept such registers of students, which is why enrolling at a university is still called matriculating.
stories.10433: The Latin "matrimonium" comes from "mater," mother. In Roman eyes, a woman married in order to become a mother. The idea has long faded, but the word for marriage still carries the mother inside it.
stories.10434: The Latin "matrix" meant a womb, from "mater," mother. From "the place where something grows," it came to mean a mould in which things are formed, then any surrounding structure. Mathematicians use it for a grid of numbers in which other values are set.
stories.10512: "Memento" is Latin for "remember!" A memento is an object that does the remembering for you. A ticket stub or a photo is a memento of a day you want to keep.
stories.10546: The Latin "meretrix" meant a prostitute, literally "a woman who earns," from the same root as "merit." Something meretricious is flashy and tempting on the surface but cheap underneath, like a lure. That's why it means almost the opposite of what it sounds like.
stories.10637: It comes from the Latin "militare," to serve as a soldier. Something that militates against a plan fights against it, making it less likely. It's often confused with "mitigate," to soften.
stories.10758: It is short for the Latin "mobile vulgus," the fickle, easily moved crowd. In the late 1600s people began clipping it to "mob," and some writers complained the short form was vulgar. A mob is a large, unruly crowd ready to act on impulse.
stories.10807: In ancient Rome, coins were made at the temple of Juno Moneta. Her title gave its name to the coins and to the workshop, which is where "money" and "mint" come from. Monetary means anything to do with money.
stories.10877: In 1910 the psychologist Henry Goddard coined "moron" as a medical label, from the Greek "moros", foolish. It was meant as a neutral clinical grade. Within a few decades the public took it up as an insult, and doctors dropped it.
stories.10890: In Old French, "mort gage" meant "dead pledge." An old English lawyer explained that the deal "dies" one of two ways: you pay it off and it ends, or you fail to pay and the land is dead to you for good. Either way, the pledge doesn't live forever.
stories.10891: In Old French, "mort gage" meant "dead pledge." An old English lawyer explained that the deal "dies" one of two ways: you pay it off and it ends, or you fail to pay and the land is dead to you for good. Either way, the pledge doesn't live forever.
stories.10895: It comes from the Latin "mors," death. Religious people once mortified the flesh, putting their desires to death through self-denial. Feeling mortified is the shame that makes you feel you could die.
stories.11059: Greek "narke" meant numbness. The same word gave the name to a numbing electric fish. Narcotic drugs are, at root, the ones that make you numb.
stories.11086: It comes from the Greek "naus," ship. The first nausea was seasickness. The word later spread to any sick feeling in the stomach, on land or at sea.
stories.11092: The Latin "navis" meant ship. The long main hall of a church, with its high arched roof, looks like an upturned ship's hull. Some also saw the church as a ship carrying its people.
stories.11421: The Latin "exsequiae" meant a funeral procession, the mourners following the body out. It got mixed up with "obsequium," obedience. Obsequies are funeral rites.
stories.11446: It comes from the Latin "occidere," to fall down, or fall toward. An occasion is something that falls your way, a chance or a moment. Special occasions are the moments that matter.
stories.11490: The Latin "officiosus" meant dutiful and obliging, eager to do favours. Being too eager to help can feel pushy, and the word slowly soured. An officious person now meddles and gives orders where they're not wanted.
stories.11506: It comes from the Latin "olere," to smell, and "facere," to make. Olfactory means to do with the sense of smell. Your olfactory nerves carry smells to your brain.
stories.11604: The philosopher Leibniz argued that we live in the best of all possible worlds; "optimum" is Latin for "the best." Voltaire mocked the idea in his novel Candide as "optimism." From that, being optimistic came to mean expecting things to turn out well.
stories.11634: The Greek "organon" meant a tool, and the parts of the body were seen as its tools, its organs. "Organic" first meant to do with organs, then with living things in general. In the 1940s it came to mean farming without man-made chemicals, using only natural ones.
stories.11640: It comes from the Latin "os," mouth, and "facere," to make: something made like a mouth. An orifice is an opening, especially in the body. It's a formal word for a hole.
stories.11669: In ancient Athens, citizens could vote to send a too-powerful person away for ten years. Each voter scratched a name onto a broken piece of pottery called an "ostrakon." No one is exiled by pottery today, but being ostracized still means being shut out by the group.
stories.11777: It comes from Greek "oxys," sharp, and "moros," dull or foolish. So the word itself is an oxymoron: "sharply foolish." It names a phrase that joins two opposite ideas, like "deafening silence."
stories.11834: Panacea was a Greek goddess of healing whose name means "all-healing." A panacea is a remedy that cures everything. It's usually used to doubt that such a cure exists.
stories.11836: It comes from the Greek "pan," all, and "demos," people: something that affects all the people. An epidemic, "upon the people," spreads through one community. A pandemic spreads across countries and the whole world.
stories.11837: It comes from the Greek "pan," all, and "demos," people: something that affects all the people. An epidemic, "upon the people," spreads through one community. A pandemic spreads across countries and the whole world.
stories.11841: The Greek "panegyris" was a festival where all the people gathered, from "pan," all. Speeches praising heroes and cities were made at these gatherings. A panegyric is still a speech or text full of praise.
stories.11842: The Greek "panegyris" was a festival where all the people gathered, from "pan," all. Speeches praising heroes and cities were made at these gatherings. A panegyric is still a speech or text full of praise.
stories.11851: Around 1790, the painter Robert Barker made the word from the Greek "pan," all, and "horama," a view. His panoramas were giant circular paintings that surrounded the viewer. Now a panorama is any wide view of everything around.
stories.11855: The Greek "pantomimos" meant "imitator of everything," a performer who acted out every role silently. In Britain, it later became a family Christmas show with songs and slapstick. To pantomime still means to act something out without words.
stories.11954: It comes from the French "passeport," permission to pass through a port, a harbour or city gate. The paper let travellers enter and leave. A passport still lets you pass through borders.
stories.11989: In ancient Rome, the "patres," fathers, were the heads of the oldest noble families, and their descendants were the patricians. Everyone else was a plebeian. Today patrician describes anyone with an aristocratic, upper-class air.
stories.11996: A Roman "patronus" was a powerful man who protected his clients like a father, from "pater," father. In return they supported him. A patron of the arts still protects and funds artists, and a shop's patrons support it with their custom.
stories.11998: To patronize first meant simply to act as a patron, to support someone. But patrons were richer and more powerful than the people they helped, and sometimes treated them like children. So to patronize also came to mean to talk down to someone.
stories.12033: In ancient Greece, a "paidagogos" was a slave who walked children, "paides," to school and watched over them. The name later passed to teachers. Today it often suggests a strict or old-fashioned teacher.
stories.12035: It comes from the Italian "pedante," a schoolmaster. Teachers who fussed over small rules and showed off their learning gave the word its flavour. A pedant now is anyone who cares too much about tiny details and correctness.
stories.12052: It comes from the Latin "par," equal. A jury of your peers is a jury of your equals. British nobles are called peers because, in old legend, a king's chief knights were all equals of one another.
stories.12073: It is French for "leaning," from "pencher," to lean, which goes back to the Latin "pendere," to hang. A penchant is a liking that you lean toward. It's usually a taste or habit, like a penchant for spicy food.
stories.12090: The Latin "pensare" meant to weigh, and also to think, because thinking was seen as weighing things up. A pensive person is quietly weighing their thoughts. The flower "pansy" comes from the French for thought, "pensee."
stories.12232: The Greek "petra" meant rock. To petrify first meant to turn something into stone, as happens to wood over millions of years. Being petrified with fear is to be so terrified you freeze, as still as stone.
stories.12302: In the 1800s, traders in China mixed English with Chinese, and the Chinese pronunciation of "business" sounded like "pidgin." "Pidgin English" was the business language of the ports. A pidgin is now any simple mixed language that people make up so they can trade or talk.
stories.12345: Around 1900 a pip-squeak was a small, unimportant person, a name that sounds as feeble as it means. In the First World War British soldiers gave the same name to a small German shell for the sound it made in flight. The shell is forgotten, but the insult lives on.
stories.12371: "Placebo" is Latin for "I shall please." It was the first word of a hymn sung at funerals, and hangers-on who sang it to win favour with grieving families became known as flatterers. So a placebo became anything given to please rather than to help, and finally a fake pill that works only because the patient believes in it.
stories.12464: The Greek "podion" meant a little foot, a base. In Roman arenas, the podium was a raised platform near the action, where important people sat. Today winners stand on a podium, and speakers speak from one.
stories.12471: It probably comes from the French "point blanc," the white spot at the centre of a target. At point-blank range you are so close you aim straight at the spot, with no need to aim higher. A point-blank refusal is just as direct: straight at you, no softening.
stories.12472: It probably comes from the French "point blanc," the white spot at the centre of a target. At point-blank range you are so close you aim straight at the spot, with no need to aim higher. A point-blank refusal is just as direct: straight at you, no softening.
stories.12514: The Roman high priest was the "pontifex," the bridge-builder, from "pons," bridge, and "facere," to make; the title later passed to the Pope. To pontificate is to speak as if you were the Pope: with total authority, at length.
stories.12540: "Port" once meant the way you carried yourself, your bearing. A portly person had a dignified, stately bearing. Since dignified older gentlemen were often heavy, portly came to mean stout.
stories.12541: The French "portemanteau" meant a coat-carrier, a travelling case that opens into two halves. Lewis Carroll used it for words that pack two meanings into one, like "slithy," from lithe and slimy. Brunch, from breakfast and lunch, is a portmanteau word.
stories.12545: A popular story says rich passengers sailing to India had tickets stamped "P.O.S.H.," for "port out, starboard home," the shady side of the ship. No such ticket has ever been found, and the story is a myth. Where posh really comes from is unknown.
stories.12621: It comes from the Latin "praeceps," headlong, head first. A precipitate act is rushed, like diving head first without looking. Rain is called precipitation because it falls from the sky.
stories.12622: It comes from the Latin "praeceps," headlong, head first. A precipitate act is rushed, like diving head first without looking. Rain is called precipitation because it falls from the sky.
stories.12680: It comes from Latin "prae," before, and "monere," to warn. A premonition is a warning that arrives ahead of time, before anything has actually happened. It is a close cousin of "admonish" and "monitor."
stories.12687: It comes from Latin "pondus," weight, and "prae," before. On old scales, the heavier side outweighs the other and sinks down. A preponderance is when one kind outweighs the rest, in number or importance.
stories.12692: It comes from the Latin "prae," before, and "posterus," after: before-after, the wrong way round. Something preposterous puts the cart before the horse. It now means absurd, completely against common sense.
stories.12820: It comes from the Latin "proficere," to make progress, to advance. A proficient person has advanced far in a skill. Today it means skilled and competent.
stories.12837: The Greek "programma" meant a public notice written in advance: "pro," before, and "graphein," to write. A concert program lists what will happen ahead of time. A computer program is the same idea: a list of instructions written out beforehand.
stories.12838: The Greek "programma" meant a public notice written in advance: "pro," before, and "graphein," to write. A concert program lists what will happen ahead of time. A computer program is the same idea: a list of instructions written out beforehand.
stories.12889: It comes from Latin "propendere," to hang forward or lean toward. A propensity is a natural leaning, a tendency to do something. It often names a habit people would rather not have.
stories.12917: It comes from the Latin "prosequi," to follow forward, to pursue. You could prosecute a war or a plan, following it through. Today it mostly means pursuing someone in court.
stories.12989: The Greek "psyche" meant breath, then the soul, the breath of life; it was also the word for a butterfly. In myth, Psyche was a mortal girl loved by Eros, the god of love. Today the psyche is the mind, with all its thoughts and feelings.
stories.12990: The word was coined in 1956 by the psychiatrist Humphry Osmond, in letters with the writer Aldous Huxley. He built it from the Greek "psyche", mind, and "delos", clear or visible: "mind-manifesting".
stories.13012: The first puddings were savoury: meat and fat stuffed into an animal's gut, like a sausage. Black pudding still keeps that meaning. Over time the cloth bag replaced the gut, sweet mixtures replaced the meat, and pudding became dessert. Where the word itself comes from, no one knows for sure.
stories.13049: The Latin "pupilla" meant a little doll. If you look into someone's eye, you can see a tiny reflection of yourself, like a little doll, in the dark centre. That's why the centre of the eye, and a young student, share the same name.
stories.13061: It comes from the Old French "purporter," to carry or contain. The purport of a message is what it carries. When something purports to be true, it claims to carry that meaning, though it may not.
stories.13062: It comes from the Old French "purporter," to carry or contain. The purport of a message is what it carries. When something purports to be true, it claims to carry that meaning, though it may not.
stories.13133: In the 1300s Venice made ships arriving from plague-hit ports wait at anchor for forty days before anyone could land. In Venetian Italian that was "quaranta giorni", forty days. The waiting period gave us quarantine, and anyone kept apart to stop a disease spreading is quarantined.
stories.13134: When the physicist Murray Gell-Mann proposed tiny particles inside protons, he wanted a funny-sounding name. He found it in James Joyce's novel Finnegans Wake, in the line "Three quarks for Muster Mark!" Fittingly, protons and neutrons each contain three quarks.
stories.13143: When astronomers in the 1960s found objects that looked like stars but blasted out radio waves, they called them "quasi-stellar radio sources": star-like, but not stars. The mouthful was quickly squeezed into quasar.
stories.13170: Queue is the French word for a tail. In English it first meant a tail on a coat of arms, then a long pigtail of hair. From there it was a short step to a line of people waiting, trailing out like a tail.
stories.13176: Quiche comes from Lorraine, a region on the border of France and Germany. The local word grew from the German "Kuchen", cake. So the most French of savoury tarts carries a German word for cake inside it.
stories.13231: Rabies is the Latin word for madness or rage, from "rabere", to rave. The disease earned the name from the wild, furious behaviour of infected animals. "Rage" itself comes from the same Latin root.
stories.13238: Radar was made up by the US Navy in 1940 from RAdio Detection And Ranging. It is one of the few everyday words that is also a palindrome: it reads the same backwards, a little like a signal bouncing back.
stories.13296: Ransack comes from Old Norse "rannsaka": "rann" meant house and "saka" meant to seek. It was first a legal search of a house for stolen goods. Today's meaning, a rough, messy search that leaves everything upturned, is the same act with the law taken out.
stories.13297: Ransom and redemption are the same word. Both come from Latin "redemptio", a buying back. Ransom travelled through Old French and was worn down along the way, while redemption kept its Latin shape. One buys back a hostage, the other a soul.
stories.13305: It comes from the French "rapporter," to bring back. Rapport is a connection where understanding passes back and forth between people. You feel it when you "click" with someone.
stories.13360: It comes from the French "rebarbatif," based on "barbe," beard: facing someone beard to beard, ready to fight. From aggressive and hostile, it came to mean off-putting and unpleasant. A rebarbative person or idea is one that repels you.
stories.13398: An old word "reck" meant to care or pay heed. A reckless person doesn't reck: they don't care about danger or what happens next. "Reck" has faded away and survives almost only in "reckless."
stories.13449: A herring smoked until it turns red has a strong smell. A popular story says it was dragged across a trail to train hounds, or to throw them off the scent. In 1807 the writer William Cobbett told of using one to mislead hounds, and the phrase came to mean any clue that leads you the wrong way.
stories.13450: For centuries English official documents were tied in bundles with red cloth tape. Untying stacks of them for every small matter became a symbol of slow, fussy officialdom. Complaints about "red tape" were common by the 1800s, and the tape itself has long gone.
stories.13508: Regatta is a Venetian word for the boat races held on the Grand Canal, where gondoliers competed. English visitors brought it home in the 1700s for any organised series of boat races.
stories.13514: It comes from the Latin "regimen," rule or guidance. It became widely used during the French Revolution, when the old order of kings was called the "ancien regime," the old regime. A regime now is a government, especially a harsh one, or a strict routine.
stories.13516: The Latin "regimentum" meant rule or government. It came to mean a body of soldiers under one commander's rule. The verb "regiment" still means to control strictly.
stories.13517: The Latin "regimentum" meant rule or government. It came to mean a body of soldiers under one commander's rule. The verb "regiment" still means to control strictly.
stories.13594: It comes from the Latin "remittere," to send back or slacken. A remiss person has let their care slacken. It means careless in doing one's duty.
stories.13845: Greek "rhapsodos" was a reciter of epic poems, literally a "stitcher of songs", from "rhaptein", to stitch. They stitched together long passages from Homer. Later, rhapsody came to mean any outpouring of passionate feeling.
stories.13851: Greek "rheuma" meant a flow. Ancient doctors believed many illnesses came from bad fluids flowing through the body. Aching joints were blamed on such a flow, and the name stayed long after the theory was gone.
stories.13860: Rickshaw is short for the Japanese "jinrikisha": "jin" person, "riki" power, "sha" vehicle. It was a human-powered vehicle, invented in Japan around 1870. English kept the end of the word and dropped the person at the front.
stories.13871: Riffraff comes from the Old French phrase "rif et raf", meaning every bit, one and all, often of things snatched up. In English it first meant odds and ends, then the people thought of as odds and ends of society.
stories.13936: The chess rook has nothing to do with the bird. It comes from the Persian "rukh", which probably meant a chariot. The castle shape of the piece is a later European idea.
stories.13940: Latin "rosarium" meant a rose garden. Medieval writers used it for a garland or collection of prayers, like a garden of flowers gathered for the Virgin Mary. The string of beads used to count those prayers took the name.
stories.13943: Roster comes from the Dutch "rooster", a gridiron for grilling. A duty list ruled with parallel lines looked like the bars of a grill, so it borrowed the name.
stories.13972: Rucksack is German: "Rücken", the back, and "Sack", a bag. Mountain climbers carried the word into English in the 1800s along with the bag itself.
stories.13973: Ruckus is an American word from the late 1800s. It is probably a blend of "ruction", an uproar, and "rumpus", a noisy disturbance. It means just what it sounds like: a noisy fuss.
stories.14024: "Ruth" was an old word for pity, from "rue," to feel sorry. Someone ruthless has no ruth: no pity for others. "Ruth" has mostly disappeared, while "ruthless" carried on.
stories.14026: The Bible tells farmers to let their land rest every seventh year, a sabbatical year, just as the seventh day is the Sabbath. Universities borrowed the idea for a long break from teaching. Traditionally it came every seventh year, though few people count so strictly now.
stories.14030: Sabot is French for a wooden clog. A popular story says angry workers threw their clogs into factory machines. More likely, "saboter" first meant to clatter about in clogs, and so to work clumsily or botch a job on purpose. Either way, the clog is at the root of sabotage.
stories.14037: In Hinduism the cow is revered and must not be harmed. Western writers in the early 1900s turned the image into a metaphor for any idea or institution treated as above criticism. The phrase says nothing about real cows, only about things nobody dares to question.
stories.14063: Salmonella is named after Daniel Salmon, an American vet. The bacterium was actually first identified by his assistant, Theobald Smith, in 1885, but the name honoured the head of the lab.
stories.14074: Salver comes from the Spanish "salva", the tasting of food or drink by a servant to show it was not poisoned before a lord ate. The tray it was presented on took the name.
stories.14080: Samurai comes from a Japanese verb meaning to serve or to wait upon. The first samurai were attendants guarding noble households. Only later did the word come to stand for Japan's proud warrior class.
stories.14107: Greek "sarkophagos" meant flesh-eating. The Greeks believed a certain limestone could dissolve a body placed inside it within weeks, so coffins made of it were called flesh-eaters. The name stayed with stone coffins of every kind.
stories.14108: The ancient Greeks spoke of a "sardonic" laugh, and the word was linked to Sardinia. One old story says a Sardinian plant twisted the faces of people who ate it into a dying grin, though no one is certain. A sardonic smile still looks like a grin hiding scorn.
stories.14129: Astrologers believed the slow, distant planet Saturn made people cold, heavy and gloomy. Someone born under Saturn was saturnine. The star-reading is gone, but the word still describes a dark, brooding face or mood.
stories.14135: It comes from the Latin "salsicia," from "salsus," salted. Meat was packed with salt to make it keep. The same salty root gives us "sauce," "salad," and "salsa."
stories.14171: Greek "skandalon" was a trap or a stumbling block, something that makes you fall. Early Christian writers used it for anything that causes someone to sin. Today a scandal is still a stumble, only now in public, with everyone watching.
stories.14188: A medieval "scavager" collected scavage, a tax on goods sold by outside merchants in towns. Over time the officer's job moved to keeping streets clean. Today a scavenger is any person or animal that lives on what others leave behind.
stories.14202: The Greek "skhisma" meant a split or tear. It was used for splits inside the church, like the great split between the Eastern and Western churches in 1054. A schism is any deep divide inside a group.
stories.14206: Schmooze comes from the Yiddish "shmuesn", to chat or have a friendly talk. In American English it took on a slightly calculating edge: warm, easy talk aimed at winning favours or contacts.
stories.14208: Scholar goes back to the Greek "schole", which meant leisure. For the ancient Greeks, free time was best spent in learning and discussion, so the word for leisure came to mean a place of study. School and scholar both grew from it.
stories.14345: Seersucker comes from the Persian "shir o shakar", milk and sugar. The cloth's stripes alternate between smooth and puckered, as different as milk and grainy sugar. The name came to English through India.
stories.14372: Seltzer is named after Selters, a German village whose natural spring water bubbles with gas. "Selterser Wasser" became seltzer in English, for any fizzy water.
stories.14378: Latin "seminarium" was a plot of land where seeds were raised into seedlings. The idea moved from plants to people: a seminary became a school where young minds, especially future priests, were grown. Seminar comes from the same seedbed.
stories.14381: The Roman Senate was a council of elders, and its name comes from Latin "senex", an old man. Senior, senile and senator share the same root. Many modern countries still call their upper house a senate.
stories.14399: The poet John Milton seems to have coined "sensuous" in 1641. He wanted a word for the pleasure of the senses, like music or colour, without the sexual meaning that "sensual" already had. That's still the difference between them.
stories.14400: The Latin "sententia" meant an opinion or feeling, from "sentire," to feel. A judge's sentence is their decision, their official opinion of the punishment. In grammar, a sentence expresses one complete thought.
stories.14401: The Latin "sententia" meant an opinion or feeling, from "sentire," to feel. A judge's sentence is their decision, their official opinion of the punishment. In grammar, a sentence expresses one complete thought.
stories.14402: The Latin "sententiae" were short, wise sayings. A sententious writer filled their work with them. Too many wise sayings sound preachy, so sententious now means pompous and moralising.
stories.14418: A Roman "sequester" was a trustee, a go-between who held disputed property until a quarrel was settled. To sequester came to mean to set something aside and keep it safe. Juries are sequestered when they are kept apart from the public.
stories.14420: A zecchino was a gold coin of Venice, named after the Zecca, the city's mint. In French it became "sequin". Later the word passed to small, shiny discs sewn onto clothes, gleaming like little coins.
stories.14428: In 1754 the writer Horace Walpole coined "serendipity" from a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries they weren't looking for. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka. Serendipity is the happy accident of finding something good by chance.
stories.14467: Shaman comes from the language of the Evenki, a people of Siberia, for a spiritual healer believed to travel to the spirit world. Russian explorers brought the word west, where it is now used for similar figures in many cultures.
stories.14471: Shanty probably comes from the Canadian French "chantier", a logging camp or the workers' cabin there. The word came to mean any small, roughly built hut. (A sea shanty is a different word, from French "chanter", to sing.)
stories.14472: A shanty was a rough cabin, probably from the Canadian French "chantier", a logging camp. Whole towns of such makeshift huts became shantytowns.
stories.14496: Sherbet comes from the Turkish and Persian "sherbet", a cool sweet drink, from an Arabic word for drink. Travellers to the Ottoman lands brought it to Europe. In different countries it now names a fruit drink, a frozen dessert, or a fizzy sweet powder.
stories.14556: In Old English a sibling was any relative. The word died out for centuries until scientists revived it around 1900 for brothers and sisters together. It filled a gap: English had no single everyday word for both.
stories.14568: There was an old word, "sideling," meaning sideways. People mistook the "-ing" for an action ending and made a new verb, "sidle," from it. To sidle is to move sideways, quietly or shyly.
stories.14601: A popular story says Roman sculptors hid cracks in marble with wax, so honest work was "sine cera", without wax. It's a charming tale but not true. Sincere comes from Latin "sincerus", clean, pure or whole.
stories.14618: Sitar comes from the Persian "seh-tar", three strings. Early versions had three strings, though the modern sitar has many more, including sympathetic strings that ring on their own.
stories.14647: A skinflint is someone so stingy they would try to skin a flint stone to make a profit from its "hide". The image is of squeezing value from something hard and worthless, which is exactly how a miser treats every coin.
stories.14668: A slapstick was a real prop: two thin wooden slats joined at one end. When an actor hit someone with it, the slats smacked together with a loud crack, while hardly hurting at all. The noisy stick gave its name to the whole style of knockabout comedy.
stories.14738: Smithereens comes from the Irish "smidirín", a small fragment, with the Irish ending "-ín" meaning little. English speakers added an extra plural, so "blown to smithereens" means blown into tiny little bits.
stories.14777: The snipe is a small bird that zigzags when it flies, making it very hard to shoot. British soldiers in India in the 1700s and 1800s called a skilled hunter of snipe a sniper. The name passed to soldiers who shoot accurately from hiding.
stories.14781: In the late 1700s a snob was a shoemaker, and in Cambridge slang a townsman, anyone not of the university. It came to mean someone of low rank who copied their betters, and then someone who looks down on others. The story that it came from "sine nobilitate", without nobility, is a myth.
stories.14785: Snorkel comes from the German "Schnorchel", a tube that let a submarine take in air while underwater in the Second World War. Swimmers borrowed the word for their own small breathing tubes.
stories.14859: Sonnet comes from the Italian "sonetto", a little song or sound. Italian poets like Petrarch perfected its fourteen lines, and English poets such as Shakespeare made it their own.
stories.14865: "Sooth" is an old English word for truth, still heard in "forsooth" and "in sooth". A soothsayer was literally a truth-sayer: someone who claimed to tell what was true, especially about the future.
stories.14895: Southpaw comes from American baseball in the late 1800s. Many ballparks were laid out so the batter faced east, which put a left-handed pitcher's throwing arm on the south side. Whether that was the real start of the word, no one knows for sure, but the name spread to left-handed boxers and everyone else.
stories.14942: The Latin "spectrum" meant an appearance or a vision, and so also a ghost. Later, the scientist Isaac Newton used "spectrum" for the band of colours in light. Spectral can mean ghostly or about a spectrum, and both meanings come from "something seen."
stories.15032: In medieval English, Prussia was called "Pruce", and goods from there were "spruce". Spruce wood, and fine Prussian leather, were famous imports. The tree took the name, and so did "spruce" for smart and neat, probably from the elegant Prussian leather jackets.
stories.15123: Stanza is Italian for a room, or a stopping place. A stanza of a poem is a room within the house of the poem, where the verse pauses before moving on.
stories.15126: Old English "steorbord" meant the steering side. Before rudders, ships were steered with a large oar over the right-hand side, and most sailors were right-handed. Ships therefore tied up with their left side against the dock, which became the port side.
stories.15186: In 1816 the French doctor René Laennec was too embarrassed to press his ear to a young woman's chest. He rolled paper into a tube and found he could hear her heart better. He named his device from the Greek "stethos", chest, and "skopein", to look.
stories.15203: Stiletto is Italian for a small, slender dagger. In the 1950s the very thin, high heels on women's shoes reminded people of the blade, and they took its name.
stories.15356: Sub rosa is Latin for "under the rose". In old European tradition the rose stood for secrecy, and a rose hung over a meeting meant nothing said there would be repeated. Plaster roses on ceilings may echo the idea.
stories.15363: The Latin "subfuscus" meant dusky, darkish brown. At Oxford University, "subfusc" is the dark formal clothing students must wear for exams. More widely, it describes anything dull and drab.
stories.15364: It comes from the Latin "subicere," to throw under. A king's subjects were placed under his power. A topic is "placed under" discussion, which is why it's a subject too.

stories.15373: The Latin "sublimis" meant raised high, lofty; where that word came from is debated. Something sublime lifts the spirit so high it seems almost beyond this world. Its opposite, the ridiculous, is famously "only one step" away.
stories.15389: It comes from Latin "sub," secretly, and "ornare," to equip. To suborn someone is to secretly equip or bribe them to do wrong. It is mostly used for getting someone to lie in court.
stories.15392: Subpoena is Latin for "under penalty". A medieval court order began with words warning that whoever ignored it would be punished. The first words of the document became its name.
stories.15403: The Latin "subsidium" meant reserve troops, the soldiers sitting behind the front line ready to help. A subsidy is help held in support. Today it is money a government gives to support a business or cost.
stories.15406: It comes from the Latin "sub," under, and "stare," to stand: what stands underneath. Philosophers used it for the real thing beneath appearances. A person of substance has something solid beneath the surface.
stories.15414: It comes from the Latin "subter," secretly, and "fugere," to flee. A subterfuge was first a secret way of escape. Now it means a trick used to get out of something or hide the truth.
stories.15418: The Latin "subtilis" meant finely woven, with threads close and thin. From fine threads, it came to mean fine and delicate in any way. A subtle difference is so fine that it's easy to miss.
stories.15439: Suede is the French word for Sweden. In the 1800s soft, velvety gloves from Sweden were sold in France as "gants de Suède", gloves of Sweden. English kept just the country's name for the leather.
stories.15479: The Latin "superbus" meant proud, even arrogant. Proud buildings and displays were grand and magnificent, and that sense took over. Superb now simply means excellent.
stories.15481: The Latin "supercilium" meant eyebrow. A supercilious person seems to look down on others with a raised eyebrow. The word paints that expression: proud and scornful.
stories.15484: The Latin "superficies" meant the surface, from "super," above, and "facies," face. Something superficial stays on the surface. A superficial wound or person doesn't go deep.
stories.15501: The Latin "superstitio" meant excessive fear of the gods; it literally means "standing over." Why it means that is debated: perhaps standing over something in awe. Today it means a belief in luck, omens or magic that has no basis in reason.
stories.15571: It comes from the Latin "suspendere," to hang up. In suspense you are left hanging, not knowing how something will end. The same root gives "suspend," "pendulum" and "pendant."
stories.15683: Tabby goes back to Attabiy, a district of Baghdad famous for a striped, shimmering silk. The cloth became "tabby" in Europe, and cats with similar wavy stripes took the name too.
stories.15686: Tabloid was a trademark of a London drug company in the 1880s for medicine compressed into small tablets. Around 1900 newspapers that squeezed the news into short, punchy stories on smaller pages took the name. Compressed medicine became compressed news.
stories.15687: It comes from the Tongan word "tapu," meaning forbidden or sacred. The English explorer James Cook brought it back from the Pacific in 1777. A taboo is something a society forbids, often without saying so out loud.

stories.15758: Tarantula comes from Taranto, a town in southern Italy. In the Middle Ages people there believed the bite of a local spider caused tarantism, a frenzy cured only by wild dancing, the tarantella. The spider in question was a wolf spider; the name later passed to the big hairy spiders of the Americas.
stories.15762: Tarmac is short for tarmacadam. In the early 1800s the Scottish engineer John Loudon McAdam built roads from layers of crushed stone. Later, tar was added to bind the stones, giving "tar-macadam", which was then trademarked as Tarmac.
stories.15800: In 1833 a temperance campaigner in Preston, England, named Richard Turner, is said to have demanded "t-t-total" abstinence, not just giving up spirits. Whether he stammered or simply stressed the T, the doubled word stuck. A teetotaler is someone who abstains totally.
stories.15807: The writer Charles Fort coined "teleportation" in 1931, describing strange objects that seemed to appear from nowhere. He joined the Greek "tele", far, with the Latin "portare", to carry. Science fiction quickly made the word its own.
stories.15873: Terminus was the Roman god of boundary stones, the markers at the edge of a field. "Terminal" means at the end or boundary. A bus terminal is the end of the line, and a terminal illness is one at the end of life.
stories.15874: Terminus was the Roman god of boundary stones, the markers at the edge of a field. "Terminal" means at the end or boundary. A bus terminal is the end of the line, and a terminal illness is one at the end of life.
stories.15878: Terra cotta is Italian for "baked earth". The name tells exactly how it is made: clay shaped and then fired. Its warm brown-orange colour is also called terra cotta.
stories.15885: It comes from the Latin "terrere," to frighten, and first meant "causing terror," like "terrifying." By the 1800s it had weakened to mean very great in size or strength, and later simply wonderful. "Awful" went through a similar journey from fear.
stories.15898: It comes from the Latin "testis," a witness. A will, or last testament, is a document made before witnesses. A testament to something is like a witness, showing proof of it.
stories.15948: Thespis was an ancient Greek poet who, the story goes, was the first to step out from the chorus and speak as a character. That made him the first actor. Ever since, actors have been called thespians in his honour.
stories.15953: Thimble comes from the Old English "thymel", from "thuma", thumb. The first thimbles were thumb-stalls, leather covers worn on the thumb while sewing. The cap moved to the finger, but the thumb stayed in its name.
stories.16056: The Latin "tintinnabulum" was a little bell. Edgar Allan Poe made "tintinnabulation" famous in his poem "The Bells", using it for the jingling, ringing sound of many bells together.
stories.16089: Tocsin comes from old French and Provençal words meaning "strike the bell". The "sin" part comes from Latin "signum", a sign, which in church Latin meant a bell. A tocsin was the alarm rung for fire or invasion.
stories.16109: The Greek "tomos" meant a slice or a cut piece. A long work was cut into separate volumes, each one a tome. Now a tome is any big, heavy book.
stories.16126: The Latin "torpere" meant to be numb. An electric fish that numbs anyone who touches it was named "torpedo," and later the weapon was named after the fish. A torpid person is sluggish, as if numbed.
stories.16164: The Greek "toxon" meant a bow, the kind that shoots arrows. Archers dipped their arrowheads in "toxikon," bow poison. Over time the bow was forgotten and only the poison stayed in the word.
stories.16176: The Latin "traducere" meant to lead across, and so to parade someone in public as a disgrace. To traduce is to damage someone's good name by telling lies about them.
stories.16261: Greek "theriake" was a medicine against the bites of wild beasts and snakes. Medieval apothecaries mixed it into sweet, sticky syrups, and the remedy's name drifted to the syrup itself.
stories.16336: The Latin "trivium" was a crossroads, where three roads met. Talk at the crossroads was small talk about everyday things. Trivia now means small, unimportant facts, the kind tested in quiz games.
stories.16337: The Latin "trivium" was a place where three roads met. Crossroads were where common people stopped and chatted about everyday things. So trivial came to mean ordinary and unimportant.
stories.16338: Latin "trivium" meant a place where three roads meet. People chatting at such crossroads talked of everyday, unimportant things. So the trivial is, at heart, crossroads talk.
stories.16344: Troll as a verb began in fishing: trolling means trailing a baited line behind a moving boat to see what bites. Online trolls do the same thing, dangling provocative bait to hook an angry reply. The cave-dwelling monster from Norse legend is a different word.
stories.16360: Trousseau is French for a little bundle, from "trousse", a bundle or kit. A bride's trousseau was the bundle of clothes and linen she took to her new home.
stories.16394: Tsunami is Japanese: "tsu", harbour, and "nami", wave. Fishermen out at sea might hardly notice the wave, then return to find their harbour destroyed. English used to say "tidal wave", although tides have nothing to do with it.
stories.16404: Tulle is named after Tulle, a town in southwestern France known for making the fine net fabric in the 1800s.
stories.16419: Turban and tulip come from the same Persian word, "dulband". European visitors thought the tulip flower looked like the wrapped headdresses they saw in the Ottoman Empire, and named the flower after them.
stories.16425: Tureen comes from the French "terrine", an earthenware dish. The odd spelling may have been influenced by a story about the Viscount of Turenne, a French marshal said to have used his helmet as a soup bowl, but no one knows for sure.
stories.16441: A turnpike was a barrier made of sharp pikes on a pivot, set across a road. Once a traveller paid the toll, it was turned aside to let them pass. Roads with such toll gates became turnpikes, the name still used for many American toll roads.
stories.16461: The rough Scottish cloth was first called "tweel", the Scots word for twill. In the 1800s a London merchant is said to have misread a handwritten "tweel" as "tweed", thinking of the River Tweed. Whatever the exact story, the river's name stuck to the cloth.
stories.16485: U-boat is short for the German "Unterseeboot", an undersea boat. The Germans used the word for any submarine, but in English it came to mean German submarines in particular, especially in the two World Wars.
stories.16491: Ukulele is Hawaiian, usually explained as "jumping flea", for the quick fingers dancing over the strings. The instrument itself came from small guitars brought to Hawaii by Portuguese workers in the 1870s. Some Hawaiians prefer another reading: "the gift that came here".
stories.16501: Umber is a natural brown earth pigment. Its name may come from Umbria, a region of Italy where it was dug, or from Latin "umbra", shadow, because of its dark colour. No one knows for sure.
stories.16595: An undertaker was anyone who undertook a job or a business. By the 1600s the word settled on the person who undertakes the arrangements for a funeral.
stories.16861: In an archery match, the upshot was the last arrow shot, the one that settled who won. From "the shot that decides it," the word came to mean the final result of anything.
stories.16910: Latin "vacca" means cow. In 1796 the doctor Edward Jenner showed that infecting people with cowpox, a mild disease caught from cows, protected them against deadly smallpox. Every vaccine since carries the cow's name.
stories.16951: The Vandals were a Germanic people who sacked Rome in the year 455. In 1794, during the French Revolution, Bishop Henri Grégoire coined "vandalisme" for the senseless destruction of art and monuments. The tribe's name became the word for anyone who wrecks things for no reason.
stories.16974: Varmint is simply "vermin", said the way it sounded in some country speech. In American English it came to mean any troublesome animal, and, half-fondly, a troublesome person.
stories.17065: It comes from the Latin "versatus," turned about, busy with something. Being well versed meant you had turned a subject over many times. That's why it means skilled and knowledgeable.
stories.17068: It comes from the Latin "verso folio," the leaf being turned. The verso is the back of a page, which you only see once you turn it. In a printed book, it is the left-hand page.
stories.17069: It comes from the Latin "vertebra," a joint, from "vertere," to turn. Vertebrae are the small bones the spine bends and turns on. Vertebrates are all the animals with such a backbone.
stories.17096: It looks as if it comes from "via," way, but it doesn't: it comes from the French "vie," life. It first described a newborn baby able to survive. A viable plan is one that can live and work.
stories.17134: In Latin a "villanus" was a worker on a villa, a country estate. In medieval times the word meant a lowly farmhand. Snobbish assumptions that low-born people were coarse and wicked slowly turned it into a word for a scoundrel.
stories.17143: It comes from the Latin "vindicta," revenge. A vindictive person wants to get back at someone who hurt them. The same root gives "vindicate," to claim back your good name.
stories.17157: The Latin "virago" meant a woman with the strength and courage of a man, from "vir," man. At first it was praise, for a brave female warrior. Over time it turned into an insult for a loud, bossy woman.
stories.17165: It comes from the Latin "virtus," power or strength. Something virtual has the power or effect of a thing without being the thing itself. A virtual meeting does what a meeting does, without people being in one room.
stories.17167: It comes from the Latin "virtus," from "vir," man: manliness, courage, strength. It came to mean any strength or excellence, then goodness. "By virtue of" keeps the older sense: by the power of.
stories.17169: It is Italian for a person of excellence, from "virtu," skill or worth, from the Latin "virtus." It first meant any learned or skilled person, then especially a dazzling musician. A virtuoso is someone with outstanding skill in an art.
stories.17303: A wardrobe was first a room where clothes were kept and guarded: a place to "ward" the "robes". Kings had a whole department called the Wardrobe. The word later shrank to a cupboard, and then stretched again to mean all the clothes you own.
stories.17579: Xeriscape was coined in 1981 by Denver Water, a water company in dry Colorado. It joins the Greek "xeros", dry, with "landscape". The word named a way of gardening with plants that need little water.
